readerTitle: Why the album came apart, then came back
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Apple iTunes Music Store, Spotify) + 가상 사례 (디자인 소프트웨어, 물류 회사, 두 팬의 숫자 예시)
insight: 번들은 단순한 묶음 할인이 아니라 부분마다 다른 고객의 가치를 한 가격으로 모으는 방법이다. 한 부분만 따로 팔기 쉬워지는 순간 묶음은 풀리고, 조각이 너무 많아지면 다시 묶인다.
misconception: 묶어서 싸게 팔면 그만큼 손해다. 번들은 고객이 원하지 않는 것까지 억지로 사게 하는 술책일 뿐이다.

sources.text: Apple press release, April 2003: launch of the iTunes Music Store, songs at 99 cents each (US)
Spotify company history: launched in Sweden in 2008
IFPI Global Music Report (streaming's share of global recorded-music revenue)
Adams, W. J. & Yellen, J. L. (1976). Commodity Bundling and the Burden of Monopoly. Quarterly Journal of Economics. (번들링 원리의 고전 연구)
두 팬 숫자 예시, 디자인 앱, 물류 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: iTunes Music Store 출시(2003년 4월, 미국에서 곡당 99센트)를 Apple 보도자료로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 "most songs"로 적었습니다(일부 곡은 앨범 전용이었음).
Spotify 출시 연도와 국가(2008년, 스웨덴)를 회사 자료로 확인하세요.
"스트리밍이 전 세계 음반 매출의 대부분"은 IFPI 최신 보고서 기준(최근 약 3분의 2 수준)으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체 수치 없이 "most"로만 적었습니다.
두 팬 계산: 팬 A 곡1 $8·곡2 $2, 팬 B 반대. 개별 $8 → 각자 한 곡 → $16. 개별 $2 → 둘 다 두 곡 → $8. 번들 $10 → 둘 다 구매(각자 총가치 $10) → $20. 개별 가격 최대 $16 < 번들 $20.

cards.title: Why the album came apart, then came back
body: For decades, if you loved one song, you usually bought twelve.
Then a store let fans buy just the song they wanted. A few years later, fans were paying a monthly fee for almost every song ever recorded. Same music, three different packages.

image.label: A vinyl album splitting into single songs, then merging into one stream
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 LP 앨범 한 장, 가운데에서 여러 개의 작은 음표 조각으로 흩어지고, 오른쪽에서 다시 하나의 흐르는 리본(스트리밍)으로 합쳐지는 장면. 실제 회사 로고, 앨범 커버, 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Customers only want one tool.
body: You sell a design app with three tools, photo, layout and video, for $30 a month. Many users say they only use one tool and ask for a $10 plan.

options.text: Split it: three separate plans at $10 each
options.feedback: Happy users, but many who paid $30 will now pay $10. You lose the revenue from people who used two tools a little and one a lot.
It protects revenue today. But users who feel they pay for unused tools are exactly who a focused rival will win over.

options.text: Keep the $30 bundle and add one single-tool plan at $15
options.feedback: Light users get a way in, and the bundle stays the better deal for anyone using two tools. You keep most bundle buyers and reach new ones.

cards.title: The album came apart, then came back bigger.
body: Before 2003, most music was sold as albums. A fan who loved one hit often paid for ten or more songs to get it.
In April 2003, Apple's iTunes Music Store began selling most songs one at a time, for 99 cents each in the US. Fans could skip the songs they didn't want.

Then the bundle returned in a new form. Spotify, launched in Sweden in 2008, sold not one album but a huge catalog for one monthly fee. Today streaming brings in most of the world's recorded-music revenue.

cards.title: Why a bundle can earn more.
body: Two fans, two songs. Fan A would pay $8 for song 1 and $2 for song 2. Fan B is the reverse. Each values the pair at $10, so a **$10 bundle** sells to both.

breakdown.label: Songs at $8 each
breakdown.detail: Each fan buys only a favorite

breakdown.label: Songs at $2 each
breakdown.detail: Both buy both, at a low price

cards.title: Bundling and unbundling
body: **Bundling** means selling several things together for one price. **Unbundling** means splitting them so customers buy only the parts they want.
A bundle works when customers value the parts differently but the whole about the same. Tastes vary piece by piece. Totals vary less. One bundle price can capture that total. Separate prices can't.

image.label: Two customers with opposite tastes reaching the same total
image.brief: 두 사람의 막대그래프. 왼쪽 사람은 "Song 1 $8" 높고 "Song 2 $2" 낮음, 오른쪽 사람은 반대. 각자 막대를 위로 쌓으면 똑같이 "$10" 높이가 됨을 강조. 간결한 인포그래픽 스타일.

cards.title: Bundles break when one piece can stand alone.
body: A bundle holds while its pieces are hard to sell separately. When that changes, a rival can sell just the part people want most. Digital files made single songs cheap to sell, so the album lost its grip.
Then the cycle often turns again. Once customers juggle too many separate pieces, someone wins by putting them back together into something simpler.
Two questions help: Do customers value the parts very differently? Could a rival sell your most-loved part on its own?

cards.title: Bundles have costs you don't see at first.
body: Bundling works best when extra parts cost little to add. A song file costs almost nothing to include. A spare part, a truck run or an hour of labor does. Pack in costly extras and the bundle discount eats your margin.
Bundles also blur feedback: you can't tell which part customers really pay for. And a bundle people feel forced into is an open door for the next unbundler.

cards.title: Now it's a warehouse and delivery firm.
body: You store, pack and ship goods for other businesses, with a separate price for each step. Small online sellers find your price list confusing. A rival now offers them one simple monthly fee for everything.

options.text: Cut each separate price below the rival's
options.feedback: You lose margin on every step, and small sellers still face a confusing list. The rival was winning on simplicity, not price.

options.text: Offer a simple package for small sellers, keep itemized prices for large shippers
options.feedback: Small sellers value the whole and dislike the details, so a bundle fits them. Large shippers know exactly what they need and would resent paying for extras.

options.text: Switch every customer to one all-in package
options.feedback: It matches the rival for small sellers. But big shippers who only need trucking now pay for storage they don't use, which invites a specialist to take them.

cards.title: Bundle when tastes differ by part. Unbundle before a rival does it for you.
body: A bundle gathers different customers' value into one price. It lasts only while no one can sell your favorite piece alone.
**Try it today:** list what you sell together. For each part, ask which customers would happily buy it alone, and what you'd charge them.
